title: Ramadan: the early meal
hook: eat before dawn, for there is blessing in it (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday: hilal, the crescent of the new moon. Your line was watch for the crescent.

Three forty-five in the morning. In old neighborhoods of Cairo or Istanbul, during Ramadan, a man may still walk the dark streets beating a small drum and calling out names, waking people up. In a suburban kitchen, a phone alarm goes off, and someone stumbles in, eyes half shut, and starts the kettle. Oats. Dates. Eggs. A lot of water. Nobody's hungry at this hour. Everyone's eating anyway. The Prophet ﷺ gave the reason in one line.
screen: `THREE FORTY-FIVE IN THE MORNING.` → `A DRUM IN THE DARK STREETS.` → `NOBODY'S HUNGRY. EVERYONE EATS.`

segments.voice: The meal is called suhur, from sahar, the last part of the night, just before dawn. The line is in Bukhari: take the suhur meal, for in suhur there is blessing. Barakah. More than a benefit: a quiet abundance, when a little turns out to be enough. The practical side is obvious, too: a long day without food or water goes better if you start it fed. But when do you stop? The Qur'an, in Surah al-Baqarah, says eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of the dawn. And there's a lovely story about that verse, also in Bukhari. A companion named Adi ibn Hatim took it literally. He put a white thread and a black thread under his pillow and kept looking at them all night, waiting to tell them apart. He couldn't. In the morning he told the Prophet, who, in one telling, teased him that his pillow must be very wide, and explained: it means the darkness of the night and the whiteness of the day. The white thread is the first line of light along the horizon. Another companion, Zayd ibn Thabit, said they ate suhur with the Prophet and then stood for the prayer; asked how long between them, he said: about as long as reciting fifty verses. So the meal was late, close to dawn. Not a midnight snack. A small, deliberate meal in the dark, the last thing before the day's long quiet.
screen: `SUHUR — FROM SAHAR, BEFORE DAWN.` · `IN SUHUR THERE IS BLESSING.` · `A WHITE THREAD AND A BLACK THREAD.` · `ABOUT FIFTY VERSES BEFORE THE PRAYER.` · then, large: `A SMALL MEAL, IN THE DARK, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Picture tomorrow morning, a little earlier than you usually wake: where the glass is, where you'll sit, drinking slowly in the dark before the day starts asking things of you. If you fast, plan your suhur the same way, simple, late, on purpose; if you don't, settle on one glass of water before anything else, and say to yourself: blessing before dawn.
Suhur. The meal before dawn in Ramadan, eaten late, for in it there is blessing. Today's word.
Your line: blessing before dawn. The first thread of light tells you when to stop. Day one hundred twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 121 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: RAMADAN: BREAKING WITH A DATE.`

howItsDone: During Ramadan, Muslims who fast wake before dawn to eat suhur, often dates, water and simple food, and stop eating and drinking at the start of dawn, when the time of fajr begins.

chat.says: Why eat in the dark during Ramadan? Wouldn't sleeping in be easier?
options: The Prophet ﷺ said that meal before dawn holds blessing, and it helps the fast.
It's eaten at midnight so the stomach is empty and rested by dawn.
It's only for people who are ill; healthy fasters wait for sunset.
chat.meaning: Bukhari: take suhur, for in suhur there is blessing. It's eaten late, close to dawn, until the first thread of light.

suhur.meaning: the meal eaten before dawn in Ramadan

sahar.meaning: the last part of the night, just before dawn

Barakah.meaning: blessing: a quiet abundance, when a little is enough

Adi ibn Hatim.meaning: a companion who took the thread verse literally

Zayd ibn Thabit.meaning: a companion who ate suhur with the Prophet ﷺ

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1923 (take suhur, for in suhur there is blessing)
Qur'an 2:187 (until the white thread becomes distinct from the black thread of the dawn)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1916, 4509–4510 (Adi ibn Hatim and the two threads)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1921 (Zayd ibn Thabit: about fifty verses between suhur and the prayer)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm. 'Your pillow must be very wide' is in Bukhari 4509/4510; framed as 'in one telling, teased him'.
The musaharati (pre-dawn drummer) is a living but declining custom in Cairo, Istanbul (davulcu) and elsewhere; stated as 'may still'.
The practice avoids any instruction to fast; it offers a glass of water as the non-fasting alternative.
